"It was prudence," the voices said, "Fear can sometimes be a good counselor," they added, humming the theme tune of the early evening TV series.
The optician was now slowing down.
The walk to Selma's house, which usually took ten minutes, suddenly seemed like an entire day's journey, a day's journey with very, very much luggage.
That was true.
The dog was the color of slushy snow, he was a washed-out gray and shaggy like an exclusive Irish Wolfhound without anything else in him.
His body was still small, but his paws were as large as bear claws, and we all knew what that meant.
Selma was still standing upright in front of the kitchen bench.
She gazed at the dog for a long time.
Then she looked at my father as if he were a gift shop.
Farmer Häubel was firmly convinced that death would be polite, just as Farmer Häubel himself had been all his life.
He was certain that death would not rip life away from him, but gently take it from his hand.
He imagined Death knocking gently, opening the door just a crack, and asking "May I?", to which Bauer Häubel would naturally reply in the affirmative.
"Of course", farmer Häubel would say, "do come in", and death would enter.
He would stand by Farmer Häubel's bed and ask, "Is it convenient for you now?"
"I can also come by at a later time.
Farmer Häubel would straighten up and say, "No no, it suits me just fine," he would add, "Let's not postpone it again who knows when you will have another chance.
And death would take a seat on the chair already set at the head of the table.
He would apologize in advance for the coldness of his hands, which he knew farmer Häubel wouldn't mind at all, and then place a hand over farmer Häubel's eyes.
The people in the village were troubled, one could see it even though they mostly tried to hide it.

This morning, just a few hours after Selma's dream, people in the village were moving as though black ice had formed on every path not only outside but also inside the houses, black ice in the kitchens and living rooms.
They moved as if their own bodies were completely foreign to them, as if all their joints were inflamed, and even the objects they handled were highly flammable.
All day long, they regarded their life and, as far as possible, that of everyone else with suspicion.

Again and again, they looked behind them to check if someone with a murderous intent might be running after them; someone who had lost their mind and therefore had nothing of significance left to lose.
They quickly turned their gaze back towards the front, for someone without sense could attack from the front-end as well.
They looked upwards to avoid any falling roof tiles, branches or heavy lampshades.
They avoided all animals, because they believed that it could break out faster from them than from humans.
They made a wide circle around the good-natured cows, who might be kicking today: they avoided the dogs, even the very old ones that could hardly stand but might still go for their throats today.
On such days, anything was possible; even an old-aged dachshund could bite through your throat.
After all, it wasn't much more far-fetched than an Okapi.
Except for Selma's sister-in-law Elsbeth, most people in the village were not superstitious.
They carelessly did all the things one should not do out of superstition.

They sat calmly under wall clocks, though with superstition one could die from that; they slept with their heads towards the door, though superstition dictates that through this very door, you will soon be carried out feet first.
They hung laundry between Christmas and New Year, which, as Elsbeth warned, in superstition is equivalent to suicide or aiding and abetting a murder.
They were not frightened when the screech owl called at night, when a horse in the stable was sweating heavily, when a dog howled at night with its head lowered.
The train journey lasted fifteen minutes, there were no stops in between.

Since our first train ride, we always played the same: We stood with our backs to the windows by the opposite train doors, Martin closed his eyes, I looked out of the train door window, which was behind Martin.
In first class, I listed to Martin everything I saw during the journey, and Martin tried to memorize it all.

That went very well, so that in the second school year I no longer described anything and Martin, with his back to the window and eyes closed, could describe almost everything that I saw through the foggy train window: "Wire factory," he said, just as we passed by the wire factory.

"What else could it have been," said Selma, adding that one could hardly confuse an okapi with any other animal.
"Nevertheless," I said, "it could have been a misshapen cow, a poorly assembled giraffe, a freak of nature.
After all, you cannot discern the stripes and reddish-brown hue so clearly at night when everything is ultimately very blurry.
"That's nonsense," Selma said, rubbing her forehead, "it's just nonsense, Luise.
She put a slice of cheese on the bread, folded it, and placed it in my sandwich box.
"Do you know exactly when you had this dream?"
"Around three o'clock," said Selma.

She had shot up, after the image of the Okapi had retreated, sitting upright in bed she had awakened and stared at her nightgown, in which she had just been standing in her dream on the Uhlheck, and then at the alarm clock.
Three o'clock.
"We probably shouldn't take this too seriously," Selma said, but she said it like a TV detective would dismiss an anonymous letter.
"What's the matter?", I asked.
"Nothing," Selma chirped, opening the fridge, she took out a packet of sliced cheese and some liver sausage, and waved them through the air.
"Little mouse," she cooed after him, and both the cooing and 'little mouse' were truly alarming.
"Cheese, please," I said, "what do you have?"
"Nothing," trilled Selma, "just as I said.
She spread butter on a slice of bread, and because she was still floundering around, she knocked the cheese off the counter with her wrist.
Now Selma stood still and looked down at the pack of cheese, as if it was something precious that had shattered into a thousand pieces.
Selma had dreamed of an okapi three times in her life, and each time someone had died afterwards.
Because of this, we were convinced that dreaming of an okapi was irrevocably linked with death.
That's how our mind works.
He can ensure in the shortest possible time that even the most divergent things firmly belong together.
For instance, coffee pots and shoelaces, or deposit bottles and Christmas trees.
When I slept downstairs at Selma's, she would tell me stories with happy endings by the bedside.
When I was younger, after the stories, I would always hold her wrist, place my thumb on her pulse and imagine that the whole world did everything in rhythm with Selma's heartbeat.

I pictured the optician grinding lenses, Martin lifting weights, Elsbeth trimming her hedge, the retailer stocking juice boxes, my mother layering pine branches, my father stamping prescriptions; and everyone was doing so precisely in time with Selma's heartbeat.
I had always been able to sleep reliably after that, but now, at ten years old, Selma thought I was too old for it.
